newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Life in Australian jobs data argue against rate cut.
newsitem.headline: Life in Australian jobs data argue against rate cut.

text.p: Key economic data suggests Australia's labour market will strengthen through 1997, reducing the need for further interest rate cuts, analysts said.
Employment levels rose by 38,400 in January, the strongest rise in 14 months, official figures showed on Thursday.
But the jobs growth was matched by an increase in people entering the labour force, leaving the politically-sensitive unemployment rate unchanged at 8.6 percent.
"It has to be regarded as a strong number and consistent with the labour market starting to look a bit better after a very weak 1996," Rothschild chief economist Ric Simes said.
"It's also consistent with the notion that 1997 overall looks a bit stronger and there's little chance of another rate cut."
The depressed labour market was a key factor behind the Reserve Bank of Australia's (RBA) decisions to cut interest rates three times between July and December last year.
But the chance of another reduction in the official rate from the current six percent has dimmed with the RBA now more confident on the outlook for 1997.

Speaking at a function on Tuesday night, RBA Governor Ian Macfarlane said the economy was starting to benefit from the rate cuts, citing improvements in housing, investment, and employment growth in recent quarters.
Analysts said Macfarlane's comments of a widely-based recovery were backed up by Thursday's data, which added to the argument that no more cuts were needed.
Employment has now risen by 92,900 in the last four months.

"When lagging indicators, such as employment, show signs of improvement, as has been the case for the past few months, the economy is well into a renewed growth phase," UBS Australia chief economist Stephen Roberts said.

"There would seem to be even less reason why the Reserve Bank would consider any further cash rate cuts in this cycle." But not all were as upbeat, arguing that a rate cut was still possible because unemployment remained high and pointing to the fact that of the January rise, 34,900 of them were part-time jobs. Economists tend to look to growth in full-time employment as a definite sign that the economy's turnaround is more than temporary.

Unemployment has been unable to move decisively under 8.5 percent since the middle of 1995. This is because the growth in employment has been matched by a similar rise in the number of people in the labour force.
Some analysts said continued jobs growth could see the unemployment rate start to edge lower through 1997.
"The Reserve Bank is likely to be impressed more by the size of the increase than by the compostion," Societe Generale chief economist John Edwards said.
"It will, correctly, ignore the fact that unemployment remained at 8.6 percent, because it contains no information about the level of economic activity," he said.
The jobs growth should also help consumer confidence, and see shoppers spending again after the retail sector experienced a very depressed period into the end of 1996.
"Money in people's hip pockets, irrespective of whether it's part-time or full-time, is still money in hip pockets," GIO Australia chief economist Akis Haralabopoulos said.
